passage:
The community centre smelled of floor cleaner and marigolds. Chandrika sat behind the voter-registration desk with a stack of forms, checking her phone every few minutes. Two weeks ago she had promised Abhinav she would run the stall so he could be at his grandmother's eightieth birthday in another town.
At ten her hostel group had messaged: a spare pass to the music festival, front section, leaving in an hour. Her thumb hovered. She could call Abhinav, say something had come up. He would understand. Probably.
She typed, "Can't, covering for someone," and put the phone face down. By four she had helped thirty-one first-time voters fill in their forms. A photo arrived from Abhinav: a cake, a grinning old lady, and "Thank you, I owe you big." She looked at it for a long time.

qa.q: How many first-time voters had Chandrika helped by four?
qa.a: She had helped thirty-one first-time voters fill in their forms.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when her thumb hovered over the phone?
qa.a: She felt torn between wanting the festival pass and her promise to Abhinav, and was tempted to invent an excuse.

qa.q: Which choice did Chandrika make, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She turned down the pass and stayed at the desk, which kept her word and makes her someone Abhinav can rely on.

qa.q: What did Chandrika's staying mean for Abhinav?
qa.a: It let him celebrate his grandmother's eightieth birthday without worry, which is why he wrote, "Thank you, I owe you big."

grounding: A young woman keeps her promise to cover a stall even when a more exciting offer appears, feeling the pull of desire against duty.

subtype: Honouring a promise at a cost [Actor]
passage:
Uday,
I know you're annoyed, so I'm writing properly instead of sending a sticker.
Yes, the beach trip sounds perfect, and yes, I was the one who pushed for it last year. But in March I promised Ma I'd be home the week after her knee operation, to do the cooking and drive her to the check-up. It's the same week.
I'll be honest: I spent two days thinking of ways to wriggle out. Ma would have said, "Go, beta, I'll manage." That's exactly why I can't. She'd manage by struggling up and down the stairs.
So I'm staying. It stings, especially knowing I'll see the group photos. Keep a seat for me on the next trip, and don't eat all the fried fish without me.
Vikas

qa.q: What did Vikas promise Ma in March?
qa.a: Vikas promised to be home the week after her knee operation, to do the cooking and drive her to the check-up.

qa.q: How does Vikas feel about missing the beach trip?
qa.a: Vikas feels stung and was tempted, spending two days looking for ways to wriggle out, but chooses the promise anyway.

qa.q: What makes the letter a good way to handle the clash?
qa.a: Vikas explains honestly, admits the temptation, and asks Uday to keep a seat next time, which protects both the promise and the friendship.

qa.q: Why might Ma say "Go, beta, I'll manage"?
qa.a: She would not want to spoil the trip for Vikas, even though managing would mean struggling up and down the stairs.

grounding: A young adult writes to Uday about keeping a promise to Ma through her recovery week, even though a longed-for trip clashes with it.

"Sangeeta, it's me. I just saw the group photos. Everyone's leaving for Rishikesh tomorrow morning."
"I know, Jahnavi. They asked me on Tuesday."
"So go! It's rafting. You've wanted to go since first year."
"I told you I'd help you move flats tomorrow."
"I can ask my cousin."
"Your cousin cancelled on you twice last month. You told me."
"Sangeeta, seriously. I'll be fine. Four boxes and a fridge."
"And a cupboard that doesn't fit through the door, and a landlord who shouts. You said you were dreading it."
"…I am dreading it."
"So I'm coming. Seven o'clock. I'll bring the tape."
"You're going to be thinking about the river all day."
"Probably. I'll survive." A pause. "Next trip, you're coming rafting with me. Deal?"
"Deal." Jahnavi's voice cracked a little. "Thank you. Really."
Sangeeta hung up, looked at the photo of the river once more, and set her alarm for six-thirty.

qa.q: Where was the group leaving for tomorrow morning?
qa.a: Everyone's leaving for Rishikesh tomorrow morning.

qa.q: How does Sangeeta feel about missing the trip?
qa.a: Sangeeta feels a real pull and some disappointment, looking at the river photo once more, but she is determined to keep her promise.

qa.q: Which choice built trust here, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the promise to help move despite the rafting trip showed Jahnavi that Sangeeta's word can be relied on, unlike the cousin who cancelled.

qa.q: What is it like for Jahnavi when Sangeeta insists on coming?
qa.a: Jahnavi feels relieved and grateful, her voice cracking, because Jahnavi was dreading the move and did not expect a friend to give up the trip.

grounding: It shows a young adult keeping a promise to help a friend move despite a more appealing trip, building reliability by staying.

passage:
I'm Leela, and in my final year I learned what a promise costs.
My friend Binita had been writing her thesis for months. I had promised to sit with her on submission night, proofread every page and walk with her to the department at eight in the morning. She was terrified of the formatting, and of doing it alone.
Then, at six that evening, the senior I'd liked all year texted: a group was going for dinner and music by the lake. Would I come?
I stared at that message for a long time. I even typed "yes." My whole chest wanted to go.
Then I thought of Binita hunched over her laptop, counting on me. I deleted the yes.
We finished at four in the morning. She fell asleep on my shoulder in the auto. Later, she told me, "You're the one I'd call in any emergency." I've kept that sentence with me since.

qa.q: What time did Leela and Binita finish?
qa.a: They finished at four in the morning.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling while staring at the senior's message?
qa.a: Leela felt a strong pull and some longing to go, torn between desire for the dinner and duty to Binita.

qa.q: What made Leela decide to stay?
qa.a: Thinking of Binita hunched over her laptop and counting on her made Leela delete the yes and keep the promise.

qa.q: How does Binita see Leela after that night?
qa.a: Binita sees Leela as someone completely reliable, the one she would call in any emergency.

grounding: It shows a young adult keeping a promise to a friend on thesis night despite a more appealing invitation, building reliability.

subtype: Honouring a promise at a cost [Actor]
passage:
Coach's log, university badminton, Wednesday.
Anand came to see me after practice. The district-level coach has invited him to pair with a stronger player for the state trials this weekend. It is a real chance. But he promised Sarita in July that he would be her mixed doubles partner in the inter-college tournament, which is the same weekend.
He was restless the whole conversation, cracking his knuckles. "If I go, she has no partner and she's out. If I stay, I might not get this chance again."
I didn't decide for him. I asked what he would want if he were in Sarita's place.
This evening he messaged: "Staying with Sarita. I asked the district coach if there's a later trial." I've written to the district coach too, to say Anand is worth watching.
Sarita doesn't know how close it was. She just saw him arrive at practice early, racket ready.

qa.q: What did Anand promise Sarita in July?
qa.a: He promised that he would be her mixed doubles partner in the inter-college tournament.

qa.q: What does Anand cracking his knuckles suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests Anand felt restless and torn, pulled between a real chance at the state trials and his duty to Sarita.

qa.q: How did the coach help Anand without deciding for him?
qa.a: The coach asked what he would want in Sarita's place, then supported his choice by writing to the district coach.

qa.q: What would have changed for Sarita if Anand had gone to the trials?
qa.a: Sarita would have had no partner and been out of the tournament, likely feeling let down.

grounding: A coach records a young adult choosing to honour a promise to a doubles partner despite a more appealing opportunity.

subtype: Honouring a promise at a cost [Actor]
passage:
Sunday night
My arms are dead. Worth it, I think.
On Wednesday I promised Maria I'd help her move out of the PG on Sunday. Her parents are in Goa, she has no one else here, and the new flat is on the fourth floor with no lift.
Then on Friday Kunal's group got free passes to the music festival. Sunday. Front section. I stared at that message for about an hour.
I even drafted, "Maria, something came up..." Deleted it. Nothing came up. Something more fun came up. That's different.
So today I carried nineteen boxes up four floors. Maria cried a bit when we finished, sitting on the floor with a steel plate of instant noodles.
She said, "I knew you'd come. You always come." That sentence is going to stay with me longer than any festival.
Irawati

qa.q: How many boxes did Irawati carry?
qa.a: Nineteen boxes up four floors.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling while staring at the festival message?
qa.a: Irawati felt tempted and torn between the free front-section passes and the promise to Maria.

qa.q: Why was deleting the 'something came up' draft the honest choice?
qa.a: Nothing had actually come up, only something more fun, so the excuse would have been a lie; keeping the word built reliability.

qa.q: What did Irawati's help mean to Maria?
qa.a: Maria, with no one else in the city, felt relieved and cared for, crying a bit and saying 'You always come'.

grounding: Shows a young adult keeping a promise to help a friend move when a more appealing festival invite arrives, and building reliability by staying.
